claims.claim: Opioid doses tend to rise as death approaches, but reviews of palliative care studies found no evidence that starting or increasing opioids to control symptoms brings death forward.
claims.supporting_passage: Sykes 2003: "We conclude that patients are more likely to receive higher doses of both opioids and sedatives as they get closer to death. However, there is no evidence that initiation of treatment, or increases in dose of opioids or sedatives, is associated with precipitation of death." Boland 2015: "Thirteen end-of-life studies, including 11 very low-quality retrospective studies, did not find a consistent association between opioid analgesic treatment and survival; this evidence comes from low-quality studies, so should be interpreted with caution."
claims.pico_timeframe: People with advanced illness (almost all cancer) in hospices and palliative care units / opioids given or increased for symptom control near death / no increase or lower doses / survival / last days to weeks of life
claims.safe_wording: Doses of morphine and similar medicines often go up in the last days of life because symptoms change. Studies of people dying in hospices and palliative care units have not found that giving or increasing these medicines to relieve symptoms shortens life.
claims.qualifications: Evidence is observational and mostly retrospective and low quality; almost all participants had cancer. Say 'have not found' or 'no consistent link'; never 'morphine does not shorten life' or 'proves'. Keep to doses adjusted to symptoms.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Portenoy 2006 found a small statistical association between higher dose and shorter survival (claim C10-25-c). Boland 2015 found that in longer-term (not end-of-life) cancer treatment six of seven studies suggested an association with shorter survival, possibly because more pain reflects more advanced cancer.

numbers.meaning: Studies in Boland 2015 systematic review that addressed survival at the end of life

claims.claim: In 238 consecutive deaths in a palliative care unit, people whose opioid doses were increased at the end of life did not live for a shorter time than those with no increase.
claims.supporting_passage: "We retrospectively analysed the pattern of opioid use in the last week of life in 238 consecutive patients who died in a palliative care unit. Median doses of opioid were low (26.4 mg) in the last 24 h of life and patients who received opioid increases at the end of life did not show shorter survival than those who received no increases."
claims.pico_timeframe: 238 consecutive patients dying in one UK palliative care unit / opioid increases in the last week of life / no increases / survival / last week of life
claims.safe_wording: In one UK palliative care unit, among 238 people who died, those whose opioid dose was increased near the end did not die sooner than those whose dose was not increased.
claims.qualifications: Single-unit retrospective study published as a letter; use as an example, not as the main evidence. Do not quote the 26.4 mg figure (units and drug not specified in the abstract).

numbers.meaning: Consecutive patients who died in one palliative care unit; retrospective

claims.claim: A larger US hospice study found higher opioid doses were statistically linked with shorter survival, but dose explained very little of the difference in how long people lived, and the authors concluded that concern about hastening death does not justify withholding opioids.
claims.supporting_passage: "Multivariate models demonstrated a significant association between shorter survival and higher opioid dose, a cancer diagnosis, unresponsiveness, and pain of <5 on a 0-10 scale, but none of these models explained >10% of the variance in time till death." ... "This analysis revealed that opioid dosing was associated with time till death, but this factor would explain very little of the variation in survival." ... "Based on these findings, concern about hastening death does not justify withholding opioid therapy."
claims.pico_timeframe: 1,306 patients in 13 US hospices, 725 with an opioid dose change / higher dose and larger increases / lower doses / days from final dose change to death (mean 12.46) / hospice stay
claims.safe_wording: The evidence is not perfectly clean: one large hospice study found a small statistical link between higher doses and shorter survival, but dose accounted for very little of the difference, and the authors said fear of shortening life should not stop pain relief.
claims.qualifications: Observational; people on higher doses are often sicker, so the link may reflect illness rather than the drug.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: This is itself the main conflicting evidence; it should be acknowledged in the post rather than hidden.

claims.claim: Tramadol blocks the reuptake of serotonin and noradrenaline, and its opioid effect comes mainly from its breakdown product O-desmethyltramadol.
claims.supporting_passage: Faria 2018: "Tramadol is a prodrug that acts through noradrenaline and serotonin reuptake inhibition, with a weak opioid component added by its metabolite O-desmethyltramadol." Coluzzi 2020: "Tramadol is the most commonly involved opioid in the reported cases of serotonin syndrome, alone or in combination with other serotoninergic medications, because of its dual mechanism of action, including inhibition of 5-HT reuptake."
claims.location: Faria 2018 abstract; Coluzzi 2020 full text, section 'Combination Therapy with Opioids: Patient Safety Issues in CKD'
claims.pico_timeframe: Pharmacology (mechanism statement)
claims.safe_wording: Tramadol is an opioid that also raises serotonin and noradrenaline levels by blocking their reuptake. Much of its opioid effect comes from a breakdown product made in the liver.
claims.qualifications: Mechanism statement; no numbers.

claims.claim: Tramadol's opioid effect depends on conversion by the liver enzyme CYP2D6, which varies widely between people, making its effect less predictable than morphine's.
claims.supporting_passage: Prescrire 2016: "The potency of codeine and tramadol is strongly influenced by the cytochrome P450 isoenzyme CYP2D6 genotype, which varies widely from one person to another. This explains reports of overdosing or underdosing after administration of standard doses of the two drugs. The potency of morphine and that of buprenorphine, an opioid receptor agonist-antagonist, appears to be independent of CYP2D6 activity." Roulet 2021: "...thus overcoming some limitations of tramadol, including the potential for pharmacokinetic drug-drug interactions and interindividual variability due to genetic polymorphisms of cytochrome P450 enzymes." Nelson 2012: "Tramadol is metabolized through CYP2D6 enzymes and all SSRIs are inhibitors of these enzymes."
claims.pico_timeframe: Pharmacology and pharmacogenetics review
claims.safe_wording: Like codeine, tramadol relies partly on a liver enzyme (CYP2D6) whose activity varies a great deal between people and is blocked by some antidepressants, so the same dose can have quite different effects in different people.
claims.qualifications: Say 'partly' or 'much of'; tramadol itself has non-opioid actions.

claims.claim: Tramadol taken with SSRIs (and other serotonergic medicines) has caused serotonin toxicity; tramadol is the opioid most often involved in reported cases.
claims.supporting_passage: Nelson 2012: "Published documentation describing the interaction between tramadol and SSRIs and its relevance to serotonin syndrome is limited to a few case reports and 1 case series. While both tramadol and SSRIs increase the amount of serotonin in the brain, the interaction is much more complicated. Tramadol is metabolized through CYP2D6 enzymes and all SSRIs are inhibitors of these enzymes. Inhibitors of CYP2D6 can increase the concentration of tramadol in the blood and thus increase its effects on serotonin in the brain, contributing to the development of serotonin syndrome." ... "Coadministration of tramadol and SSRIs has caused serotonin syndrome." Coluzzi 2020: "Tramadol is the most commonly involved opioid in the reported cases of serotonin syndrome, alone or in combination with other serotoninergic medications, because of its dual mechanism of action, including inhibition of 5-HT reuptake."
claims.pico_timeframe: Case reports, case series and pharmacovigilance summaries
claims.safe_wording: Tramadol taken with some antidepressants has caused serotonin toxicity (agitation, twitching, shaking, sweating, fever). Among opioids, tramadol is the one most often named in reported cases.
claims.qualifications: Evidence is case reports and pharmacovigilance, so frequency is unknown; do not state a rate. Some SSRIs also block CYP2D6 and reduce tramadol's pain relief (Roulet 2021 citation snippet via Scite), so the combination can bring both more side effects and less relief. Roulet 2021 full-text passage (Scite citation snippet): "The bioactivation of tramadol by CYP2D6 is an important source of variability due to drug interaction. The analgesic efficacy of tramadol can be significantly reduced by CYP2D6 inhibitors, such as some SSRIs or terbinafine."

claims.claim: Tramadol has been linked with low sodium, low blood sugar and seizures, adverse effects not shared to the same degree by other opioids.
claims.supporting_passage: Prescrire 2016: "In addition, tramadol can cause a serotonin syndrome, hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia and seizures." ... "Tramadol has additional adverse effects unrelated to its opioid effects." Roulet 2021: "tapentadol is likely to result in less exposure to serotoninergic adverse effects (nausea, vomiting, hypoglycaemia)" ... "its residual serotonergic activity (serotonin syndrome, seizures)". Owsiany 2019: "There is also concern for increased risk of seizures and central nervous system adverse effects in older adults with prolonged tramadol use."
claims.location: Prescrire 2016 abstract; Roulet 2021 abstract; Owsiany 2019 full text, section 4
claims.pico_timeframe: Reviews of trial and pharmacovigilance data
claims.safe_wording: Tramadol can also cause low sodium, low blood sugar and seizures, effects that come from its non-opioid actions.
claims.qualifications: 'Can cause' is supported by reviews; frequencies come only from the Fournier studies (C10-18-e, -f).

claims.claim: In a UK primary care cohort of 332,880 people starting tramadol or codeine, hospital admission for low sodium in the first 30 days was 4.6 per 10,000 person-months with tramadol versus 1.9 with codeine (adjusted HR 2.05).
claims.supporting_passage: "Using the UK Clinical Practice Research Datalink and Hospital Episodes Statistics database, a population-based cohort of 332,880 patients initiating tramadol or codeine was assembled from 1998 through 2012." ... "The incidence rates of hospitalization for hyponatremia were 4.6 (95% CI, 2.4-8.0) and 1.9 (95% CI, 1.4-2.5) per 10,000 person-months for tramadol and codeine users, respectively. In the adjusted model, the use of tramadol was associated with a 2-fold increased risk of hospitalization for hyponatremia, compared with codeine (adjusted HR 2.05; 95% CI, 1.08-3.86)."
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults starting tramadol or codeine for non-cancer pain, UK primary care / tramadol / codeine / hospital admission for hyponatraemia / first 30 days after starting
claims.safe_wording: In UK GP records of over 330,000 people starting tramadol or codeine, about 4.6 in every 10,000 people taking tramadol for a month were admitted to hospital with low sodium, compared with about 1.9 for codeine: roughly twice the rate, but still uncommon.
claims.qualifications: Absolute rate first; 'per 10,000 person-months' means per 10,000 people each taking the drug for one month. Wide confidence interval (1.08 to 3.86) from few events. Adults of all ages, not only older people; observational (association, adjusted by propensity score).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Only one large study; restricted sub-cohort gave HR 3.54 (1.32 to 9.54), consistent in direction. Do not quote both HRs.

numbers.meaning: Adults starting tramadol or codeine, UK CPRD, 1998 to 2012
Absolute rates of hospital admission for hyponatraemia, tramadol vs codeine, first 30 days
Relative rate, tramadol vs codeine, propensity-score adjusted

claims.claim: In the same UK data, starting tramadol was linked with more hospital admissions for low blood sugar than starting codeine, especially in the first 30 days.
claims.supporting_passage: "The cohort included 334,034 patients, of whom 1105 were hospitalized for hypoglycemia during follow-up (incidence, 0.7 per 1000 per year) and matched to 11,019 controls. Compared with codeine, tramadol use was associated with an increased risk of hospitalization for hypoglycemia (OR, 1.52 [95% CI, 1.09-2.10]), particularly elevated in the first 30 days of use (OR, 2.61 [95% CI, 1.61-4.23]). This 30-day increased risk was confirmed in the cohort (HR, 3.60 [95% CI, 1.56-8.34]) and case-crossover analyses (OR, 3.80 [95% CI, 2.64-5.47])." ... "Additional studies are needed to confirm this rare but potentially fatal adverse event."
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults newly treated with tramadol or codeine for non-cancer pain, UK / tramadol / codeine / hospital admission for hypoglycaemia / whole follow-up and first 30 days
claims.safe_wording: The same UK research group found that people starting tramadol were more likely to be admitted to hospital with low blood sugar than people starting codeine, mainly in the first month. It is rare.
claims.qualifications: Nested case-control design (odds ratios); no absolute excess risk can be derived from the abstract, so do not turn the ORs into 'X times' statements or absolute numbers. The 0.7 per 1000 per year incidence is for the whole cohort (both drugs), not tramadol.

numbers.meaning: Incidence of hospitalisation for hypoglycaemia in the whole cohort (tramadol and codeine users together)

claims.claim: There is no evidence that tramadol (or codeine) is less risky than morphine at its lowest effective dose, and its effects vary more between people.
claims.supporting_passage: "In practice, when opioid therapy is needed, there is no evidence that codeine, dihydrocodeine or tramadol is less risky than morphine at its lowest effective dose. Compared to morphine, the efficacy of these drugs varies more from one patient to another, and their multiple pharmacokinetic interactions can be difficult to manage. There is also a sometimes unpredictable risk of serious over-dose. Tramadol has additional adverse effects unrelated to its opioid effects. Weak opioids require at least as much vigilance as morphine, despite the major differences in their reputation and regulation."
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults needing opioid analgesia; review of trials and pharmacovigilance
claims.safe_wording: Calling tramadol a 'weak' opioid does not make it a safer one: an independent review found no evidence that it is less risky than a low dose of morphine, and its effects are less predictable.
claims.qualifications: Frame the 'low dose of another opioid' point as a prescribing judgement, and add that morphine itself needs adjusting when kidney function is reduced (see C10-19). Evidence gap, not proof of equal or greater harm.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Morphine accumulates in reduced kidney function (C10-19-a), so the alternative depends on the person.

claims.claim: Tramadol and its active breakdown products are cleared mainly by the kidneys, so its dose needs adjusting when kidney function is reduced.
claims.supporting_passage: Coluzzi 2020: "With the regard to the use of the “weak opioid” tramadol, it is relevant to point out that 90% is renally excreted and its half-life may increase up to twofold in CKD patients." Owsiany 2019: "Tramadol (immediate release) is not recommended for usage in older chronic kidney disease patients. Tramadol and its active metabolites are predominantly renally cleared."
claims.location: Coluzzi 2020 full text, 'Pharmacological Update'; Owsiany 2019 full text, section 4
claims.pico_timeframe: Pharmacokinetics in chronic kidney disease
claims.safe_wording: Tramadol leaves the body mainly through the kidneys, so kidney function belongs on the pre-prescribing check along with the antidepressant list, sodium and any history of seizures.
claims.qualifications: Reviews differ on whether to avoid (Owsiany) or dose-adjust (Coluzzi); say 'check and adjust', not 'contraindicated'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Coluzzi says older people with GFR over 30 need no dose change up to 300 mg; Owsiany recommends avoiding immediate-release tramadol in older people with CKD.

numbers.meaning: Share of tramadol excreted by the kidneys (Coluzzi 2020 narrative review)

claims.claim: The AGS Beers Criteria 2023 list tramadol among drugs to use with caution because of hyponatraemia or SIADH.
claims.supporting_passage: Not found: PMC full text (PMC12478568) opened, but the criteria tables were not rendered in the text returned; the narrative does not mention tramadol.
claims.pico_timeframe: n/a
claims.safe_wording: Do not cite the Beers Criteria for tramadol.
claims.qualifications: Non-essential.

claims.claim: Morphine is broken down in the liver into M3G and M6G, which leave the body through the kidneys; when kidney function is reduced they build up, and M6G build-up can cause toxicity.
claims.supporting_passage: Coluzzi 2020: "In the liver, morphine is metabolized into two primary metabolites named 3 (M3G) and 6 glucuronide (M6G), which are eliminated via kidney pathways. In CKD condition, a significant renal retention of active or toxic metabolites occurs; for this reason, morphine is contraindicated in cases of renal failure, because the M6G accumulation may cause neurotoxic symptoms." Owsiany 2019: "Specifically, greater accumulation of morphine and its metabolite, morphine-6-glucuronide (M6G), was found with decreased renal function." ... "Morphine and its metabolites are renally cleared, and in patients with significant renal impairment, these compounds are likely to accumulate."
claims.location: Coluzzi 2020 full text, 'Pharmacological Update on Opioid Analgesics in CKD'; Owsiany 2019 full text, sections 2 and 4
claims.pico_timeframe: Pharmacokinetics; adults and older adults with chronic kidney disease
claims.safe_wording: Morphine is broken down in the liver into active products that leave the body through the kidneys. When the kidneys work less well, these products build up with repeated doses.
claims.qualifications: Mechanism is well established; clinical evidence on how often it causes harm is very low quality.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Owsiany 2019: two studies found no relationship between morphine metabolite levels and adverse events (see C10-19-f).

claims.claim: Build-up of morphine and its metabolites in people with reduced kidney function can cause drowsiness, confusion, twitching (myoclonus), slowed breathing, nausea and constipation.
claims.supporting_passage: Owsiany 2019: "Because of the increased risk for adverse events, such as nausea, confusion, constipation, sedation, respiratory depression, and myoclonus, safe prescription of opioids is critical in the older, non-dialysis chronic kidney disease patient population." ... "Accumulation of morphine and its metabolites can cause adverse events such as nausea, vomiting, confusion, severe constipation, and cognitive dysfunction." Dubs 1999 (case report): "On the 7th day of morphine administration she became somnolent and breathing became markedly depressed, indicating overdosage" ... "As M6G is excreted by the kidney, its concentration rises in renal failure and can lead to severe intoxication."
claims.location: Owsiany 2019 full text, Introduction and section 2; Dubs 1999 abstract (English)
claims.pico_timeframe: Older adults with non-dialysis CKD (review); one case with chronic renal failure (case report)
claims.safe_wording: In a person with reduced kidney function who is on regular morphine, new drowsiness, confusion, muscle twitching or slowed breathing can be signs that it is building up.
claims.qualifications: Hallucinations were NOT found in the opened sources for morphine in renal impairment: leave them out. 'Twitching is an early sign' is NOT supported: do not say it. 'Develops over days' rests on pharmacology plus a single case report (day 7): say 'with repeated doses' or 'can appear after several days', not a fixed timescale.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The Owsiany introduction lists these effects for opioids in older people with CKD generally, not morphine alone.

claims.claim: European palliative care guidance based on a systematic review advises that morphine side effects in renal impairment can be managed by lengthening the dosing interval, reducing the 24-hour dose or switching opioid, and names fentanyl, alfentanil and methadone as least likely to cause harm; the evidence is very low quality.
claims.supporting_passage: "All of the studies identified have a significant risk of bias inherent in the study methodology and there is additional significant risk of publication bias. Overall evidence is of very low quality." ... "Fentanyl, alfentanil and methadone are identified, with caveats, as the least likely to cause harm when used appropriately. Morphine may be associated with toxicity in patients with renal impairment. Unwanted side effects with morphine may be satisfactorily dealt with by either increasing the dosing interval or reducing the 24 hour dose or by switching to an alternative opioid."
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults with cancer pain and renal impairment / opioids / other opioids / toxicity and pain relief / not specified
claims.safe_wording: European palliative care guidance suggests a lower daily dose, a longer gap between doses, or a switch to an opioid less dependent on the kidneys, such as fentanyl or alfentanil, with specialist advice.
claims.qualifications: Evidence is very low quality and from cancer pain; recommendations rest on pharmacokinetics and experience. Name only fentanyl and alfentanil (methadone needs specialist use). Do not name oxycodone as a safe swap (C10-19-d).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Sande 2016 found fentanyl/alfentanil/sufentanil recommendations rest on pharmacokinetics with very little clinical evidence.

numbers.meaning: Studies included in King 2011 systematic review

claims.claim: Oxycodone's breakdown products are also cleared by the kidneys and can accumulate, so it is not a straightforward substitute.
claims.supporting_passage: Coluzzi 2020: "its hepatic metabolism produces multiple metabolites, including the noroxycodone and oxymorphone (further metabolized to noroxymorphone), which could accumulate in patients with renal failure, since oxycodone elimination is relatively impaired in ESRD patients." Owsiany 2019: "Oxycodone and its active metabolites are cleared renally, and this clearance may be greatly reduced in older, renally-impaired patients."
claims.location: Coluzzi 2020 full text; Owsiany 2019 full text, section 4
claims.pico_timeframe: Pharmacokinetics in CKD
claims.safe_wording: Switching to oxycodone does not remove the problem: its breakdown products also depend on the kidneys.
claims.qualifications: Both reviews say oxycodone can be used with dose adjustment and monitoring.

claims.claim: Kidney function falls with age, and creatinine-based eGFR can overestimate kidney function in people with little muscle.
claims.supporting_passage: Owsiany 2019: "Given the decreased kidney function associated with aging and chronic kidney disease, these patients are at increased risk for drug accumulation and adverse events." Hanna 2024: "Creatinine-based estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) may overestimate kidney function in patients with sarcopenia. While cystatin C-based eGFR (eGFR) is less affected by muscle mass, it may underestimate kidney function in patients with obesity." ... "After adjustment for potential confounders, CT-defined sarcopenia and high adiposity were both associated with >30% eGFR discordance (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.90, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.12-3.24; aOR 2.01, 95% CI 1.15-3.52, respectively)" ... "A spline model demonstrated that as skeletal muscle index decreases, the predicted difference between eGFRand eGFRwidens considerably."
claims.location: Owsiany 2019 abstract; Hanna 2024 abstract (Background and Results; subscripts cr/cys lost in the PubMed text)
claims.pico_timeframe: 545 adults with cancer, mean age 63 / CT-defined sarcopenia / no sarcopenia / cystatin C eGFR more than 30% below creatinine eGFR / cross-sectional
claims.safe_wording: A creatinine result in the normal range can hide low kidney function in someone with little muscle, because creatinine comes from muscle. In a study of people with low muscle mass, creatinine-based estimates often read well above cystatin C-based estimates.
claims.qualifications: Hanna 2024 studied people with cancer (mean age 63), not frail older people specifically, and compared two estimates rather than measured GFR. The 'creatinine comes from muscle' explanation is standard physiology but was not stated verbatim in the opened sources beyond 'less affected by muscle mass'; keep it brief. Prefer 'can' to 'often' for the general statement.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: C06-B2 (claim C06-19-e) records that in very old people on DOACs the choice of kidney equation did not change outcomes; the size of the problem for opioid dosing is unmeasured.

numbers.meaning: Adjusted odds of more than 30% discordance between cystatin C and creatinine eGFR with sarcopenia (do not quote in a public post)

claims.claim: The clinical evidence linking morphine, kidney function and side effects is limited and partly conflicting.
claims.supporting_passage: Sande 2016: "There is lack of consensus within the existing literature on the relationship between morphine, creatinine levels and morphine-related side effects. Based on the current evidence, morphine should be used with caution; however, more evidence is needed." Owsiany 2019: "Alternatively, two studies found no relationship between serum concentrations of morphine, M6G, and morphine-3-glucuronide (M3G) and pain intensity or adverse events."
claims.location: Sande 2016 abstract, Conclusions; Owsiany 2019 full text, section 2
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults with cancer pain and renal impairment (18 studies, n = 2,422)
claims.safe_wording: The studies are small and do not all agree, so the advice rests mainly on how the drug is handled by the body and on clinical experience.
claims.qualifications: State as a named limitation, not a reason to ignore the risk.

numbers.meaning: Sande 2016 systematic review, cancer patients with renal impairment

claims.claim: Among 18,343 surgical patients (mean age 52) in two US hospitals, 35.7% used no opioids in the 24 hours before discharge, and 45.6% of those were still prescribed opioids to take home.
claims.supporting_passage: "Among the 18 343 patients (10 069 women and 8274 men; mean age, 52.2 years) who underwent 21 452 surgical procedures, there was wide variation in the amount of opioids prescribed at hospital discharge given a postoperative patient's 24-hour predischarge opioid use. A total of 6548 patients (35.7%) used no opioids in the 24 hours prior to hospital discharge; however, 2988 of these patients (45.6%) were prescribed opioids at hospital discharge, suggesting potential overprescription."
claims.pico_timeframe: Adult and paediatric postoperative inpatients (mean age 52.2), two US hospitals, 2014 to 2016 / 24-hour pre-discharge opioid use / amount prescribed at discharge / cross-sectional
claims.safe_wording: In a US study of over 18,000 surgical patients (average age 52), about 1 in 3 took no opioid in the last 24 hours before going home, yet almost half of that group were still given an opioid prescription to take home.
claims.qualifications: Must state: surgical patients, average age 52, US hospitals; not older medical inpatients. 'Potential overprescription' is the authors' label; some may have needed pain relief at home.

numbers.meaning: Postoperative patients, two US hospitals, 2014 to 2016
Mean age
Used no opioids in the 24 hours before discharge
Of those 6,548, the number prescribed opioids at discharge

claims.claim: The amount of opioid prescribed at discharge varied widely for the same level of use in the last 24 hours.
claims.supporting_passage: "...there was wide variation in the amount of opioids prescribed at hospital discharge given a postoperative patient's 24-hour predischarge opioid use." ... "Opioids are not regularly prescribed in a patient-specific manner to postoperative patients."
claims.pico_timeframe: As C10-13-a
claims.safe_wording: The amount prescribed to take home varied widely between people who had used the same amount in hospital.
claims.qualifications: Surgical population.

claims.claim: In general surgical patients, opioid use at home after discharge was best predicted by the number of opioid doses taken the day before discharge.
claims.supporting_passage: "For patients discharged after POD 1, in multivariate analysis, the number of opioid pills used at home was associated with the number taken the day before discharge (p < 0.0001) and patient age (p = 0.006), but not the type of surgery. Forty-one percent of patients took no opioids the day before discharge, 33% took 1 to 3, and 26% took more than 4 pills. Eighty-five percent of patients' home opioid requirements would be satisfied using the following guideline: if no opioid pills are taken the day before discharge, no prescription is needed; if 1 to 3 opioid pills are taken the day before discharge, then a prescription for 15 opioid pills is given at discharge; and if 4 or more pills are taken the day before discharge, then a prescription for 30 opioid pills is given at discharge. If these guidelines were used, the number of opioid pills prescribed would decrease by 40%." ... "For patients admitted after surgical procedures, post-discharge opioid use is best predicted by usage the day before discharge."
claims.pico_timeframe: 333 general surgical inpatients discharged home, one US centre; chronic opioid users excluded / doses the day before discharge / home opioid use measured by questionnaire and phone
claims.safe_wording: In a US study of general surgical patients, the number of opioid doses taken the day before discharge was the best guide to how much they used at home. A simple rule based on that count would have met the needs of 85 in 100 patients and cut the tablets prescribed by 40%.
claims.qualifications: Single US centre, 333 surgical patients, not older-person specific. 85 in 100 means about 15 in 100 would have needed more: present 'none used' as a prompt to ask about pain at home, not an automatic no.

numbers.meaning: General surgical inpatients in the study
Took no opioids the day before discharge
Patients whose home needs would be met by the day-before-discharge rule
Reduction in opioid tablets prescribed if the rule were used

claims.claim: A count of the last 24 hours is a rough guide: in a plastic surgery cohort, a 24-hour model predicted home opioid use much less well than a model using the whole inpatient course.
claims.supporting_passage: "The POP model had the strongest association (R2 = 0.899; P < 0.0001) between model output and postdischarge opioid consumption when compared to a procedure-based (R2 = 0.226; P = 0.025) or a 24-hour (R2 = 0.152; P = 0.007) model."
claims.pico_timeframe: 116 plastic and reconstructive surgery inpatients with stays of 2 to 8 days / personalised model vs 24-hour model vs procedure-based model / home opioid use reported at 4 weeks
claims.safe_wording: The 24-hour count is a starting point, not a formula: look at the trend over the whole stay and ask the person what activity at home will involve.
claims.qualifications: Small single-centre study; the 'look at the trend' advice is a judgement informed by it.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Conflicts in part with Hill 2018, which found day-before use the best predictor among the factors it tested.

claims.claim: In older adults, opioid use is linked with falls, fall injuries and fractures.
claims.supporting_passage: "Thirty studies, providing 34 relevant effect sizes, met the inclusion criteria for this meta-analysis. Overall, opioid use was significantly associated with falls, fall injuries, and fractures, with effect sizes ranging from 0.15 to 0.71. In meta-regressions, no selected factors explained heterogeneity." ... "While heterogeneity is present, results suggest an increased risk of falls, fall injuries, and fractures among older adults who used opioids."
claims.pico_timeframe: Older adults / opioid use / non-use / falls, fall injuries, fractures / observational studies
claims.safe_wording: In older people, opioid use is linked with more falls and fractures.
claims.qualifications: Observational; association, not proof of cause; do not quote the pooled effect sizes (log scale). An unneeded take-home supply adds risk without benefit is a judgement, not a measured finding.

claims.claim: The evidence comes from surgical patients (mean age 52 in the largest study); applying the counting habit to older medical inpatients is a judgement.
claims.supporting_passage: Chen 2018: "Among the 18 343 patients (10 069 women and 8274 men; mean age, 52.2 years) who underwent 21 452 surgical procedures..." Hill 2018: "We studied 333 inpatients discharged to home after bariatric, benign foregut, liver, pancreas, ventral hernia, and colon surgery."
claims.pico_timeframe: Surgical inpatients
claims.safe_wording: These studies were in surgical patients, mostly younger than the people on a geriatric ward; using the count for older medical patients is sensible practice, not something these studies tested.
claims.qualifications: Required caveat in every version.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No study of older medical inpatients found.

claims.claim: In a UK randomised trial of 608 adults on strong opioids for chronic non-cancer pain, a supported group programme helped far more people stop opioids (29% vs 7% at 12 months) and pain interference with daily life was no worse than with usual care.
claims.supporting_passage: Sandhu 2023: "Of 608 participants randomized (mean age, 61 years; 362 female [60%]; median daily morphine equivalent dose, 46 mg [IQR, 25 to 79]), 440 (72%) completed 12-month follow-up. There was no statistically significant difference in PROMIS-PI-SF-8a scores between the 2 groups at 12-month follow-up (-4.1 in the intervention and -3.17 in the usual care groups; between-group difference: mean difference, -0.52 [95% CI, -1.94 to 0.89]; P = .15). At 12 months, opioid discontinuation occurred in 65 of 225 participants (29%) in the intervention group and 15 of 208 participants (7%) in the usual care group (odds ratio, 5.55 [95% CI, 2.80 to 10.99]; absolute difference, 21.7% [95% CI, 14.8% to 28.6%]; P < .001)." Sandhu 2026 (HTA): "The findings only apply to people willing to consider opioid reduction and may not apply to a more complex secondary care population. The results may not be applicable to people using very high opioid doses." ... "The I-WOTCH intervention helps substantially more people stop opioids than best usual care without adversely affecting pain interference."
claims.location: Sandhu 2023 abstract, Results; Sandhu 2026 abstract, Limitations and Conclusions
claims.pico_timeframe: 608 adults (mean age 61) on strong opioids for chronic non-malignant pain, 191 English general practices / 3 group days plus nurse support for tapering over 12 months / usual care (booklet and relaxation CD) / pain interference (PROMIS) and self-reported stopping / 12 months
claims.safe_wording: In a UK trial in general practice, people on strong painkillers for long-term pain who got group sessions and nurse support to reduce them were much more likely to have stopped a year later (29 in 100, against 7 in 100 with usual care). Pain getting in the way of daily life was no worse than in the usual-care group.
claims.qualifications: Mean age 61: few very old or frail people. Participants were willing to consider reduction; opioid use self-reported. 'No worse' = no clear difference (the trial did not show pain improved). Absolute figures first.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Serious adverse events were somewhat more common with the intervention (claim C10-24-b).

numbers.meaning: Adults randomised, English primary care
Trial population
Stopped opioids at 12 months, intervention vs usual care; absolute difference 21.7 percentage points
Between-group difference in pain interference score at 12 months (no clear difference; MCID 3.5)

claims.claim: In the same trial, serious adverse events were 8% with the programme vs 5% with usual care, and 1% of the programme group needed extra care for possible withdrawal symptoms.
claims.supporting_passage: "Serious adverse events occurred in 8% (25/305) of the participants in the intervention group and 5% (16/303) of the participants in the usual care group. The most common serious adverse events were gastrointestinal (2% in the intervention group and 0% in the usual care group) and locomotor/musculoskeletal (2% in the intervention group and 1% in the usual care group). Four people (1%) in the intervention group received additional medical care for possible or probable symptoms of opioid withdrawal (shortness of breath, hot flushes, fever and pain, small intestinal bleed, and an overdose suicide attempt)."
claims.pico_timeframe: As C10-24-a
claims.safe_wording: Reducing was not free of risk even with support: serious health problems were reported in 8 in 100 people in the programme and 5 in 100 with usual care.
claims.qualifications: Not all serious adverse events were due to reduction; no significance test is given in the abstract for this difference.

numbers.meaning: Serious adverse events, intervention vs usual care, 12 months
Intervention group needing extra medical care for possible or probable withdrawal symptoms

claims.claim: A systematic review of 67 studies found very low quality evidence that pain, function and quality of life may improve after long-term opioid dose reduction.
claims.supporting_passage: "Sixty-seven studies (11 randomized trials and 56 observational studies) examining 8 intervention categories, including interdisciplinary pain programs, buprenorphine-assisted dose reduction, and behavioral interventions, were found. Study quality was good for 3 studies, fair for 13 studies, and poor for 51 studies." ... "Among 40 studies examining patient outcomes after dose reduction (very low overall quality of evidence), improvement was reported in pain severity (8 of 8 fair-quality studies), function (5 of 5 fair-quality studies), and quality of life (3 of 3 fair-quality studies)." ... "Very low quality evidence suggests that several types of interventions may be effective to reduce or discontinue LTOT and that pain, function, and quality of life may improve with opioid dose reduction."
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults on long-term opioids for chronic pain / dose reduction or discontinuation strategies / various / pain, function, quality of life, withdrawal, adverse events / variable
claims.safe_wording: Older, weaker studies of people who reduced long-term opioids more often reported that pain and daily function improved than worsened, but most of those studies were small, uncontrolled and poor quality.
claims.qualifications: Say clearly that the studies were weak. Many involved intensive pain programmes, so improvement may come from the programme rather than the lower dose. Use I-WOTCH (C10-24-a) as the lead evidence.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: I-WOTCH (the best trial) found no difference in pain interference, i.e. not worse but not better.

numbers.meaning: Frank 2017 systematic review

claims.claim: In a large US cohort of people on stable higher-dose long-term opioids, tapering was linked with more emergency or hospital visits for overdose or withdrawal and for mental health crisis, and faster reductions were linked with higher risk (corrected figures).
claims.supporting_passage: Corrected abstract (Scite record of the corrected article): "Posttapering patient periods were associated with an adjusted incidence rate of 6.3 overdose events per 100 person-years compared with 4.9 events per 100 person-years in non-tapered periods (adjusted incidence rate difference, 1.4 per 100 person-years [95% CI, 0.7-2.1]; aIRR, 1.28 [95% CI, 1.15-1.43]). Tapering was associated with an adjusted incidence rate of 7.4 mental health crisis events per 100 person-years compared with 4.3 events per 100 person-years among nontapered periods (adjusted incidence rate difference, 3.1 per 100 person-years [95% CI, 2.1-4.1]; aIRR, 1.74 [95% CI, 1.50-2.01]). Increasing maximum monthly dose reduction velocity by 10% was associated with an aIRR of 1.05 for overdose (95% CI, 1.03-1.08) and of 1.14 for mental health crisis (95% CI, 1.11-1.17)." Erratum letter (Fenton 2022, 10.1001/jama.2022.0231): "After reanalyzing the data with corrected programming codes, the results showed that dose tapering remained significantly associated with both overdose and mental health crises, although the incidence rate ratios were reduced from 1.68 (95% CI, 1.53-1.85) to 1.28 (95% CI, 1.15-1.43) for overdose and from 2.28 (95% CI, 1.96-2.65) to 1.74 (95% CI, 1.50-2.01) for mental health crisis." Original abstract: "Although these findings raise questions about potential harms of tapering, interpretation is limited by the observational study design."
claims.location: Corrected abstract, Results (via Scite); erratum letter JAMA 2022;327(7):687
claims.pico_timeframe: 113,618 US adults on stable doses of 50 MME/day or more for 12 months (mean age about 58) / tapering of 15% or more / no tapering / ED or hospital encounters for overdose or withdrawal, and for mental health crisis / up to 12 months
claims.safe_wording: Cutting down can carry risk if it is rushed or imposed. In US insurance records, periods after a dose reduction had about 6 emergency visits for overdose or withdrawal per 100 people a year, against about 5 without reduction, and about 7 mental health crises per 100 a year against about 4. candidates.reason: Essential claims supported: doses rise near death and reviews found no evidence that starting or increasing symptom-guided opioids precipitates death (Sykes 2003; Boland 2015 systematic review, very low-quality evidence); illustrative UK series (Thorns 2000). The post must also acknowledge the qualifying evidence: Portenoy 2006 found a small statistical link between higher dose and shorter survival that explained very little of survival, and its authors concluded fear of hastening death should not stop opioids. Use 'studies have not found' / 'no consistent link', never 'morphine does not shorten life'; say the studies are observational and mostly in people with cancer. The NICE NG31 claim was not verified and must not be used. Keep strictly to symptom relief (values concern: no reference to assisted dying or double effect).

All essential claims supported: dual serotonin/noradrenaline plus opioid mechanism (Faria 2018; Coluzzi 2020); CYP2D6-dependent, variable effect (Prescrire 2016; Roulet 2021; Nelson 2012); serotonin toxicity with SSRIs (case-report level; tramadol the opioid most often involved); low sodium, low blood sugar and seizures (Prescrire; Roulet; Owsiany); hyponatraemia rates 4.6 vs 1.9 per 10,000 person-months, HR 2.05 (1.08 to 3.86) in UK adults of all ages (Fournier 2015); hypoglycaemia ORs (Fournier 2015, nested case-control, no absolute figure). The Beers 2023 tramadol entry could not be verified (tables not rendered) and must not be cited. Give the absolute hyponatraemia rates beside 'about twice' and say it is uncommon. The 'low dose of another opioid' point must be framed as judgement and must not recommend morphine to people with reduced kidney function (link to C10-19). Suggested pre-prescribing check supported by these sources: antidepressant list, sodium, seizure history, kidney function.

Core mechanism and action are supported (M3G/M6G cleared by kidneys and accumulate: Coluzzi 2020, Owsiany 2019; dose reduction, longer interval or switch, with fentanyl/alfentanil least likely to cause harm: King 2011, very low-quality evidence; oxycodone also accumulates; creatinine eGFR can overestimate kidney function with low muscle: Hanna 2024). But three elements of the candidate are not supported: hallucinations as a sign (not found in opened sources), 'twitching is an early sign that is easy to miss' (not found), and a fixed 'over days' time course (single case report only). The evidence base is small and partly conflicting (Sande 2016; Owsiany 2019) and must be named.
candidates.revised_angle: Open with the observable situation: a person with reduced kidney function on regular morphine who becomes newly drowsy, confused, twitchy or breathes more slowly; explain that morphine's active breakdown products leave through the kidneys and build up with repeated doses; the action is to check kidney function (remembering that a normal creatinine can hide low function in someone with little muscle), then lower the dose, lengthen the interval or switch to an opioid less dependent on the kidneys such as fentanyl or alfentanil with specialist advice; oxycodone is not a simple swap. Name the limitation: the advice rests mainly on pharmacology and small studies. Drop hallucinations and the 'early sign' claim.

candidates.reason: Essential claims supported: Chen 2018 figures (18,343 surgical patients, mean age 52.2; 35.7% used no opioids in the last 24 hours; 45.6% of those were prescribed opioids at discharge; wide variation); Hill 2018 shows home use was best predicted by the day-before-discharge count and a count-based rule met home needs of 85% (so about 15% would need more, which supports the judge's 'prompt, not automatic no'); opioids linked with falls and fractures in older adults (Yoshikawa 2020, observational). Required qualifications: surgical populations, mean age 52, not older medical inpatients (extension is judgement); the 24-hour count is a rough guide (Zhang 2022: R2 0.152 for a 24-hour model). The visual's 'None used' box should read as a question about pain at home, not 'no prescription'.

The candidate's lead claim rests on Frank 2017, whose evidence is very low quality. A stronger source was found: the UK I-WOTCH randomised trial (Sandhu 2023; HTA 2026), in which supported reduction led 29% vs 7% to stop opioids with no difference in pain interference, though serious adverse events were 8% vs 5%. The harm side is supported by Agnoli 2021, but that article was CORRECTED (Feb 2022): the PubMed abstract still shows the original, withdrawn figures; only the corrected figures (6.3 vs 4.9 overdose or withdrawal events and 7.4 vs 4.3 mental health crises per 100 person-years; faster reduction linked with higher risk) may be used. No tapering rate or UK guidance could be verified, so the visual's '[N] weeks' must go. All evidence is from people averaging 58 to 61 years; the post must say the studies included few very old people.
candidates.revised_angle: Lead with the UK I-WOTCH trial: with group sessions and nurse support, many more people came off strong opioids and pain did not interfere with daily life any more than with usual care (no clear difference, not an improvement). Balance it equally with the risk of rushed or imposed reduction from the corrected US cohort data (association, not proof of cause). Close on an agreed, slow pace with regular review and support, without a specific rate. Mention the weaker older studies (Frank 2017) only as 'earlier, weaker studies more often reported improvement'.
